paras: The "Possum Hunters" warning to J. K. McGoodwin was a written threat left in August 1915 at the brickyard of McGoodwin, a brick manufacturer in Princeton, Kentucky, ordering him to get rid of his Black laborers or lose his life. McGoodwin dismissed his Black workers at once. Newspapers outside Kentucky noted the case chiefly because McGoodwin was described as the father of the United States minister to Venezuela, and they reported it as part of a wave of night riding in Caldwell and Christian counties.

In mid-August 1915, reports from Princeton and Hopkinsville described masked bands, called night riders or "possum hunters," operating in Caldwell and Christian counties in western Kentucky. In northern Christian County, fifteen masked and armed men visited the homes of white and Black residents, whipped several people and left notices for residents to leave the community. A Lexington dispatch said all Black residents of the affected sections had been ordered to leave "on pain of death" and attributed the trouble to the employment of Black workers "where white men formerly were."

At Princeton, a warning note and a bundle of thorn switches were left at McGoodwin's brickyard. According to the local dispatch, the notice was signed "Possum Hunters" and read, as printed: "Yon [You] will get rid Of the negroes you Ore [are] working. Heed this warning and save your neck." The Lexington dispatch described the note as "tied in switches" and said it ordered McGoodwin to discharge all his Black employees "or be hanged." McGoodwin complied, and the Princeton report said he "at once dismissed his negro force." The papers give neither the date the note was left nor the number or names of the workers.

No arrests were reported in connection with the note, and the Lexington dispatch stated that state authorities had so far taken no action against the night riders. The coverage does not show what became of the dismissed workers.

The story reached the press through three channels within two days. A Nashville wire dated August 19, built on advices from Princeton and Hopkinsville, closed with the McGoodwin paragraph and ran in the Newark Evening Star, the Washington Evening Star and, on August 22, the Richmond Virginian; the Harrisburg Telegraph printed a shortened version without it. Its headlines, such as "Night Riders in Kentucky" and "'Possum Hunters' Feared," emphasized the masked bands rather than the Princeton threat, and each version identified McGoodwin by his son's diplomatic post.

A Lexington dispatch in the East St. Louis Daily Journal took a broader view under the headline "Kentucky Race War Feared," reporting that some Black residents were fleeing to Indiana while others had armed themselves. Closer to home, the Hopkinsville Kentuckian printed a brief Princeton dispatch under the headline "Princeton Man Bluffed," the only version to quote the notice and its signature; no Black newspaper coverage of the Princeton note was found.

Accounts differ in the wording of the threat: the local dispatch quotes the notice as telling McGoodwin to "save your neck," while the Lexington dispatch paraphrases it as an order to discharge his workers "or be hanged." The wire versions also give the son's name variously as Preston B. McGoodwin, Preston M. McGoodwin and "Preston Goodwin."

bases: An anonymous band signing itself 'Possum Hunters' left a written warning with thorn switches ordering an employer to get rid of his Black laborers on threat of death, amid a night-rider campaign to drive Black people out (A1, A2, A6).
A local Princeton dispatch (A6), a Lexington dispatch (A1) and a Nashville wire (A2) independently report the note, the switches and the discharge of the Black workers, differing only in detail.

accounts.label: Local Princeton dispatch
accounts.gist: McGoodwin received a notice signed 'Possum Hunters' with thorn switches, threatening him for employing Black laborers and telling him to 'save your neck'; he at once dismissed his Black force.

accounts.label: Nashville wire
accounts.gist: A warning note and a bundle of thorn switches were left at McGoodwin's brickyard and he discharged his Black laborers, as part of renewed night riding in Caldwell and Christian counties.

accounts.label: Lexington dispatch
accounts.gist: The note, tied in switches, ordered him to discharge all his Black employees or be hanged; he did, amid a feared 'race war' caused, the dispatch said, by Black workers holding jobs white men formerly held.

framing.detail: The East St. Louis Daily Journal headed the story 'Kentucky Race War Feared' and attributed the trouble to Black employment in jobs white men formerly held, noting that state authorities had taken no action.
Eastern papers ran the Nashville wire under 'Night Riders in Kentucky' and '"Possum Hunters" Feared', with the McGoodwin item as a closing paragraph identifying him by his son's diplomatic post.
The Hopkinsville Kentuckian printed the local dispatch under 'Princeton Man Bluffed', quoting the notice in full.
